item.title: Sinking profits turn China's $3.5 trillion stock rout into a deeper trap
item.description: The world's second-largest equities market has lost $3.5 trillion in value from a peak in May, data compiled by Bloomberg show ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Jeanny Yu Pessimism has gripped Chinese stocks, with no end in sight for a deepening selloff as investors confront the realities of an economy that’s weak enough to erode corporate profits but not to trigger forceful new stimulus. The world’s second-largest equities market has lost $3.5 trillion in value from a peak in May, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The rout intensified last week, pushing the onshore benchmark CSI 300 Index into a bear market and a technology sector gauge in Hong Kong toward erasing all its gains since Beijing’s sweeping growth support package two years ago. At the heart of investor gloom is an unsettling realization that a protracted consumption slump and the race-to-the-bottom mentality among businesses is taking a heavier toll on earnings across industries from banks to electric car makers and AI model developers. Further darkening the outlook is the growing perception that Chinese leaders are in no rush to jump-start an economy that is slowing but at a tolerable speed.  “It is too early to conclude that the worst is over,” said Ulrich Urbahn, head of multi-asset strategy and research at Berenberg. “The biggest concern remains profitability: China’s strength in production and exports is not translating consistently into stronger domestic demand, pricing power and corporate earnings.” The third-quarter reporting season got off a disappointing start, with battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd., or CATL, suffering a profit miss that was symptomatic of both weak demand and fierce competition.   The consensus 2026 earnings forecasts for the MSCI China Index members has declined by over 4% since the end of March, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The Hang Seng Tech Index, dominated by Chinese Internet firms mired in e-commerce price wars, has seen profit projections plunge more than 13% during the period. Yet even against the lowered expectations, the MSCI China’s constituents that have released results have missed consensus forecasts by an average of 9%, set for the second worst quarterly miss in two years, according to Bloomberg calculations. Among them, AI infrastructure builder China Mobile Ltd.’s January-September net profit tumbled 8% on year amid cost pressures, while major materials firm Ganfeng Lithium Group Co. also missed estimates on falling prices.  “CATL is the best poster child of what’s going on: great innovative company that’s doing great things but a victim of cut-throat competition and margin squeeze,” said Jason Lemire, chief investment officer at Bold Wealth Partners. “Competition is encouraged and generally brutal in China, not shareholder friendly.” Profit SqueezeThe earnings pressure has left companies, particularly China’s Internet behemoths that are in a tense race to fund costly AI infrastructure build-outs, increasingly out of cash. That has forced some of them to tap the equities market to raise funds, such as Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s $10 billion follow-on stock sale, which further diluted share value.  “I’d always weigh Japan, Korea and Taiwanese firms over China because they have better earnings,” said Stanley Tang, senior portfolio manager at Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management. “If you ask me what China can do, hard to think of any - even further localization of tech may not help to boost share prices.”   Weakening investor confidence is also showing up via other measures. Turnover in China’s onshore stock market is hovering near the lowest level since July last year, while the outstanding amount of margin trades — bets funded by borrowed cash — fell to the least in a year. To be sure, the slumping market has already prompted authorities to mobilize state funds known as the national team to prevent stock prices from spiraling out of control.  Meanwhile, the recent rout has boosted the appeal of Chinese equities to some investors. Bridgewater Associates’ China arm, for one, said it has turned “prudently optimistic” on local stocks, saying the declines in the third quarter were largely driven by liquidity while valuations aren’t high. It also argued that policy favors long-term capital formation and more money may flow into equities given low bond yields.  Still, skepticism abounds that while the national team’s rescue efforts may be a temporary fix, the market’s long-term prospect remains dim given policymakers’ reluctance to adopt big-bang stimulus measures to accelerate economic growth.  China’s third-quarter gross domestic product grew 4.5% from a year ago, nudging expansion in the first nine months back into the government’s annual goal of 4.5%-5%. That target-meeting performance has given authorities more reason to stick to a drip-feed style of growth support, without compromising fiscal discipline or further reducing historically low borrowing costs. “Policymakers are comfortable with the nature of economic growth,” said William Bratton, head of cash equity research for Asia Pacific at BNP Paribas. “As a result, either because they’re consciously keeping it in reserve or because philosophically they don’t believe in it, there’s no urgency to use fiscal measures to promote large scale consumption.”

Home / World News / Trump weighs fresh Iran strikes as he keeps prospect of a deal open

Trump weighs fresh Iran strikes as he keeps prospect of a deal open He recently said on social media he would not hit Iran again before the Nov 3 midterm elections

Anxiety has been growing in Iran and elsewhere that the US or Israel will resume attacks before or just after Tuesday's elections in Israel or the US midterm elections (Photo: Reuters)

AP Washington 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 9:26 AM IST

Listen to This Article

US President Donald Trump bristled when asked how far he was from a possible attack on Iran.   He recently said on social media he would not hit Iran again before the Nov 3 midterm elections.   "Do you really think I'm going to tell you if I'm going to do it?" Trump told reporters here on Saturday.   "And there's a possibility I will. There's also a possibility we'll have a nice, big, beautiful agreement," he said in response to a question.   Trump repeated his assertion that Iran wants to make a deal, "but the problem is, will they hold the deal?" Also Read

Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused Washington of disrupting negotiations to end the war but said he still believes "we have to go and finish it".

In comments aired on state television, he said Iran's supreme leader had instructed Iranian officials to "go and finish it (the deal)," but "these scoundrels broke the rules of the game. We were holding talks, and they disrupted them".   Anxiety has been growing in Iran and elsewhere that the US or Israel will resume attacks before or just after Tuesday's elections in Israel or the US midterm elections.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Yemen's Houthis say they targeted Saudi oil sites, attacks reported in Aden

Yemen's Houthis say they targeted Saudi oil sites, attacks reported in Aden Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden

The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran | Image: Reuters

Reuters 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 8:28 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.   On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war, Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden.   Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements, though they reported missile debris falling near the site of one of the purported oil targets. It was not immediately clear if any of the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted.

Saudis report debris from intercepted missiles   Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline. Also Read

IndiGo extends cancellation of flights to Saudi Arabia: Indian Embassy

14 nationals on board a yacht off Yemen coast safe, says Indian embassy

India coordinating with airlines for return of Saudi pilgrims: MEA

Indian national killed, 2 hurt in attack on Saudi Arabia's Dammam airport

Saudi Arabia seeks access to foreign strategic oil reserves for Aramco

He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.   The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif.   Saudi Civil Defence said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Mecca and Medina regions, home to Islam's holiest sites visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims every year.

It said parts of the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, while debris also fell in areas in Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. It was not clear if that was linked to the Houthis' reported targeting of the Rabigh oil refinery.   Shortly after that, Houthis denied that they attacked Mecca and Medina, saying that their operations "target Saudi oil facilities and military bases."   The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.   The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.

In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognised government said two of the Houthis' missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.   Houthi spokesman Saree said the group's forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilisation there.   There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.   Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah.

About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.   The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Soldiers guard centre of Milan as thousands protest across European cities

Soldiers guard centre of Milan as thousands protest across European cities The protests encompass a broad range of issues from education and corruption to anti-war movements, pensions and housing

Members of the military walk by a boarded-up Saint Laurent store, ahead of a protest called by the October 17 Movement against the rising cost of living, in Milan, Italy (Photo: Reuters)

AP Milan 6 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 8:06 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Thousands of young people marched on Saturday through the streets of several Italian cities, including Milan, Rome and Turin, as authorities deployed large numbers of police and soldiers in a largely-successful bid to stave off a repeat of the violent clashes and looting that marred similar protests last week. The demonstration in Milan remained peaceful, but there were brief clashes with police in both Rome and Turin. In Milan, thousands of young people marched the streets as soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up, but by late afternoon, most shops had opened, Italian media reported. Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week. In Milan, police detained several minors as a preventive measure, media reported.

While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities on Saturday from Milan to Rome to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana. Also Read

Police, protesters clash in Paris as 410,000 demonstrate across France

Italy sends more soldiers to Milan as European cities brace for protests

AISA chief Neha Bora refuses to sign peace bond, questions curbs on dissent

SC panel to hear Jantar Mantar protest violence complaints on Oct 29, 30

France deploys 70,000 security personnel as new protests raise riot fears

The protests encompass a broad range of issues from education and corruption to anti-war movements, pensions and housing. Army vehicles and boarded-up luxury stores in Milan   In Milan, huge crowds of mostly young people gathered as night fell, chanting insults to Meloni and holding aloft banners such as "No to lies of the state". A group of protesters dumped manure outside Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic, oversized electricity bill, images broadcast on local television showed.

The 500 soldiers deployed to Milan came in addition to hundreds already stationed there, supporting about 5,000 police and other security personnel. Authorities used drone surveillance, checks at railway stations, rapid-response units and online monitoring for potential calls to violence. A mayoral hopeful, Pierfrancesco Majorino, who announced his candidacy on Thursday, joined the marchers and remarked how peaceful the day was, according to Italian media. He will contest a centre-left primary in early 2027. Milan's centre-left Mayor Giuseppe Sala, who has held the role since 2016, is not running again. Many stores, particularly luxury boutiques within Milan's fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows. The Apple store also shut down and remained shut even as others reopened.

Rioters last weekend smashed their way into stores, targeting sneakers, athletic wear and sporting goods on streets that run off the city's central Duomo square. Security measures extended beyond the city centre over concerns protesters could move into other neighbourhoods. The protesters ended their march peacefully on Saturday evening outside the Milan Polytechnic, more than three kilometres (two miles) from the city centre. Officials said on Saturday they were investigating a 30-year-old freelance journalist said to be the "mastermind" of the newly-formed October 17 movement, which has been the main driver of the recent protests in Italy. Milan police say last week's violence and looting involved about 2,000 very young protesters, many of them "naturalised, second-generation Italians", alongside foreign nationals. Over two days, police arrested 45 people, including 34 minors.

A group of about 30 far-right activists, described as hooligans linked to Inter Milan soccer club, made a brief appearance chanting anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans but were isolated by police. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said the soldiers deployed on Saturday were only recently allowed to use plastic restraint ties and only in areas around train stations, not throughout the city. They are not authorised to carry pepper spray or tasers, he said. Protesters try to force entry into Colosseum in Rome   Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.

A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards. Elsewhere, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters. "I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study ... and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities," said Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association. A separate anti-war march took place in central Rome. Organisers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.

But it was these marchers who briefly clashed with police near the Piazza della Repubblica, even as organisers were trying to hold the crowd back using batons and tear gas. In the end, the protesters pulled back when a water cannon was turned on. They retreated to a location about half a kilometre away. Clashes and buildings set on fire in Albania   In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom set government buildings on fire and threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 officers patrolled the streets on Saturday. For over a week, protesters have hurled rocks, flares, firebombs and fireworks at police who have used batons and tear gas in clashes in the city centre.

High school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama. A separate protest organised by the opposition outside the prime minister's office turned violent earlier, with some activists lighting fires on the street. Rama said on Saturday his government was preparing a response to the students' demands and called them to a dialogue. He warned that violent protesters will face penalties. Pensions and housing spark Madrid and Lisbon protests   Thousands of retirees and others marched peacefully in Spain's capital on Saturday to demand public pensions are not meddled with.

"They are threatening us with privatising pensions. It is just another thing they want to profit from," said Maria Jose Benito, 68. The protests came ahead of next month's snap election as Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's Socialist Party criticised the conservative opposition Popular Party for making overtures about privatising public pensions. Spain also has been roiled by protests this fall around the issue of housing, as rental and home costs have risen in recent years beyond what many Spaniards can afford. Taking their cue from Spaniards, protesters in Lisbon demanding affordable housing marched across the city on Saturday. They have also targeted recent measures announced by the government of Prime Minister Luis Montenegro that include easing the cap on yearly rent increases and facilitating the eviction of tenants who fail to pay rent.

Montenegro defends the measures, saying that they aim at reinforcing trust between tenants and landlords and boosting the rentals market. Protesters claim that the measures are not balanced and put tenants in a more vulnerable position.
